storylines.label: Large Language
storylines.latest_title: Show HN: Dev-Mem – Local-first SQLite knowledge graph for AI coding agents

editorial.tldr: This thread was regrouped from a speculative-decoding run into a broad bucket of 77 papers and posts sharing the phrase "large language", mostly arXiv, from Nov 6. Its largest strands are hallucination fixes, which moved from preference alignment to decode-time methods, eval-validity papers, and RAG and agent-memory designs.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 26: Dev-Mem, a Show HN tool, gives Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and OpenCode a local SQLite store of past decisions and failed approaches, a day after Merlin-Bench found 10 frontier LLMs struggle to produce verifier-accepted proofs.
editorial.why_it_matters: The useful signal for platform teams is in two strands: RAG citations can misstate provenance undetected, and eval scores move with rater drift and prompt framing, so both retrieval attribution and regression evals need their own checks.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before trusting RAG citations, sample answers and check that the cited passage actually supports the claim; when a regression eval moves, re-score an older baseline with today's judges or rubric first to rule out rater drift.

storylines.label: Nemotron 3.5
storylines.latest_title: Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference

editorial.tldr: Nemotron 3.5 launched in October with day-0 vLLM support for Super VL, added speech with Transcribe, and picked up an AWS EKS guide by Oct 29. In November AWS put Super VL into SageMaker JumpStart, and two arXiv papers followed: a 4GB small model for conversational agents and an RL post-training study on Super.
editorial.whats_new: NVIDIA released three synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe and a DFlash speculator for faster inference for Nemotron 3.5 Parse, its document-parsing model, on Nov 26.
editorial.why_it_matters: Nemotron 3.5 is turning from one hosted model into a family you can fine-tune and serve yourself, from a 4GB agent model to a 120B multimodal model, each with open data or recipes.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you parse PDFs or scans in a RAG pipeline, fine-tune Parse on your own documents with the released recipe and measure the DFlash speculator's latency before swapping out your current parser.

status.detail: Super VL is one-click on SageMaker JumpStart; the family now includes a small agent model and a Parse model with open datasets and a speculator.

storylines.label: Multi-agent Systems
storylines.latest_title: Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems

editorial.tldr: This is a theme thread, not one event: three weeks of mostly arXiv work on what breaks when LLM agents run as a team, starting with KV-cache memory cost and orchestration. It split into security against malicious peers, tracing which agent caused a failure, and latent agent-to-agent channels that LatentLens and Chasm found unhelpful or exploitable.
editorial.whats_new: Hugging Face (Nov 26) published reproducible recipes for training multi-agent teams, the first about $50 on two H200s, a day after MeterRouter reported top multi-agent accuracy at 82% lower cost on five benchmarks.
editorial.why_it_matters: The thread has moved from what fails in agent teams to what they cost: per-query routing under a dollar budget and cheap team training make cost a tunable you can benchmark, not a fixed overhead of going multi-agent.
editorial.take_for_builders: Record per-query token cost next to accuracy in your multi-agent evals, and keep KV-cache or latent hand-offs between models behind the same injection guards as text messages until Chasm-style defenses ship.

storylines.label: Inkling Mini
storylines.latest_title: Show HN: Rust agent with an Inkling 2 Mini inference engine for Apple Silicon

editorial.tldr: Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini on Nov 20: a looped multimodal MoE with about 26B total parameters, roughly 3B active per token, and a 1M-token context. vLLM shipped day-0 serving on Blackwell, Hopper and DGX Spark the same day, with a Docker image.
editorial.whats_new: Five days after launch, an agent-driven tuning run pushed single-user decode on one RTX PRO 6000 from 136 to 190.6 tok/s, and a Rust engine now serves the model on Apple silicon behind an OpenAI-compatible API.
editorial.why_it_matters: A 26B MoE with about 3B active parameters and 1M context now has serving paths on datacenter GPUs, one workstation card and Macs, so local coding-agent backends no longer need a hosted API.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you run a local coding-agent backend, benchmark Inkling 2 Mini with the vLLM Docker image on your own hardware before adopting the community tuning numbers.

status.detail: Open-weight release with vLLM support at launch; community tuning and non-CUDA runtimes followed within a week.

storylines.label: Benchmarking Real-World
storylines.latest_title: $μ$-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-User Task Completion in Shared Interaction Voice Agents

editorial.tldr: This is a research trend, not one event: unrelated arXiv papers since Nov 6 each test agents on real sessions, real tools or real fixes instead of standalone tasks. It began with memory poisoning and voice-agent speaker separation, then moved to long-horizon infra work, researcher workspaces, privacy-aware code review (Nov 13) and agentic video (Nov 18).
editorial.whats_new: μ-Bench (Nov 25) tests voice agents serving several users at once across 800 simulated cases in 20 domains; proprietary agents reach about 62–65% success while open-weight models stay below 20%.
editorial.why_it_matters: Each paper argues that standalone task scores overstate how agents behave on stateful, multi-party, long-horizon or compliance-sensitive work, and μ-Bench puts a 40-point gap between proprietary and open-weight voice agents on exactly that kind of work.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you ship a voice agent on an open-weight model, test it on multi-speaker sessions before rollout; if your agents persist memory, add an eval that replays a poisoned instruction across sessions.

storylines.label: Case Study
storylines.latest_title: How Much Do Coding Agents Over-Edit, and Why? An Empirical Study of Unneeded Edits in Repository-Level Agent Patches

editorial.tldr: This is not one story: the six papers share only the phrase "case study" or "empirical study" in their titles. They form a loose November run of arXiv work that measures how agents and models actually behave, covering where long-horizon errors enter, what token spend tracks, KV cache reuse, benchmark throttling and web-element hallucination.
editorial.whats_new: The newest paper reverts each unit of a coding-agent patch and reruns the tests to find unneeded edits, across 7,660 Copilot CLI trajectories from 18 models on SWE-bench Verified and DeepSWE.
editorial.why_it_matters: The common thread is measurement: several of these papers test whether a number teams already rely on (pass rate, token spend, benchmark score) means what they assume it means.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you gate coding-agent patches on passing tests alone, add a diff-size or revert-and-retest check, because a passing patch can still carry edits the tests never needed.

storylines.label: Speculative Decoding
storylines.latest_title: DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target's Sparsity

editorial.tldr: Early November papers reworked the drafter: acceptance-length losses (D-REAL, REAL Loss) and pruned or fork-aware block-diffusion draft trees. By Nov 20 the work reached serving and real output formats, with Callo decoding on invalidated KV and Grammar-as-a-Draft speeding JSON and tool-call outputs in vLLM.
editorial.whats_new: DFly2 (Nov 25) drops the drafter's own KV cache and reuses the target's cache and sparse index selections, accepting more tokens per step than DFlash and DSpark on long contexts.
editorial.why_it_matters: Long-context agent traffic makes a separate drafter cache a memory cost; DFly2-style sharing and grammar-forced drafting target the workloads platform teams actually serve, not chat benchmarks.
editorial.take_for_builders: If your agents emit JSON or tool calls, benchmark grammar-forced drafting on your vLLM structured-output path first, and try temperature-calibrating your existing draft model before swapping drafters.

storylines.label: Activation Steering
storylines.latest_title: TASK Memory: Beyond Text-Only Memory with Activation Steering and Knowledge Editing against Memory Hallucination

editorial.tldr: A Nov 13 paper argued that SAE steering applied to every token pushes representations off-distribution and proposed per-token gating that follows the generation trajectory. A Nov 19 paper then recast RL post-training of diffusion transformers as activation steering, tying a costly training step to an inference-time intervention.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 25 paper, TASK memory, pairs each text memory note with activation steering and a removable knowledge edit, reporting memory-ignoring errors cut to at most 1.5% across ten model-dataset cells on frozen LLMs.
editorial.why_it_matters: Activation steering is moving from a behavior knob into agent memory, so teams fighting memory hallucination on open-weight models get a no-fine-tuning option beyond better retrieval and prompting.
editorial.take_for_builders: If your agent ignores or misuses its stored notes on a frozen open-weight model, add a memory-ignoring error rate to your evals now so you can compare TASK-style steering against your current retrieval setup.

storylines.label: On-Policy Distillation
storylines.latest_title: Collect for Coverage, Replay with Evidence: Adaptive and Efficient On-Policy Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents

editorial.tldr: On Nov 8 an arXiv paper measured how much quantized or asynchronous rollout mismatch on-policy distillation (OPD) tolerates. Over Nov 9-10, three papers pushed OPD into agent training: recovering skills lost to best-checkpoint GRPO selection, picking teacher reference trajectories for multi-turn tool use, and training coding-agent file-memory habits.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 25: CARE-OPD, an arXiv paper, replays trajectory prefixes during on-policy distillation of long-horizon agents and reports 59.5% on SWE-bench Verified with 45% less training time than asynchronous online OPD.
editorial.why_it_matters: OPD is becoming a standard agent post-training step, and rollout generation is its dominant cost; CARE-OPD and the mismatch study both target that cost directly.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you distill long-horizon or coding agents on-policy, benchmark prefix replay against your async online OPD before buying more rollout compute; CARE-OPD's 45% saving is self-reported and unreplicated.

status.detail: A cluster of arXiv papers adapting OPD to agents and cutting its rollout cost; no independent replication yet.

storylines.label: Reinforcement Learning
storylines.latest_title: Maco-RL: Scaling Agent Capabilities with Mixed-Task Reinforcement Learning

editorial.tldr: This is a theme thread of mostly arXiv papers, not one developing story. Since Nov 6 it has tracked RL for agents (multi-agent training, RL-learned memory, rollout cost), the finding that RL tool-use gains can raise tool hallucination, and Nov 23 work tracing gains to verified state and specific agent roles.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 25: a paper reports coding agents that read an environment's source code write policies matching or beating conventional RL, and Maco-RL lifts Qwen3.5-27B from 43.6 to 60.1 on five benchmarks with mixed-task RL.
editorial.why_it_matters: If you post-train or operate tool-using agents, this cluster names where RL pays off and what it costs: rollout throughput, tool hallucination, reward design, and when code-writing agents can skip RL, though nearly every result is author-reported.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before funding an RL run for an agent, test whether a coding agent can write the policy from your environment's code, and score any RL-tuned model on tool-hallucination rate and per-role behavior next to task success.

storylines.label: Recursive Self-Improvement
storylines.latest_title: RoboEvo$^2$: Recursive Robot Self-Improvement via Harness-Policy Co-Evolution

editorial.tldr: Early November's recursive self-improvement (RSI) papers had agents rewrite their own harness (prompts, tools, memory, control loop) with the base model frozen, and added a benchmark, a statistical acceptance test, and a multi-agent science version. From Nov 18 the loop moved into the weights: BaseRSI, Piccolo, and test-time TT-RSI each fold self-generated gains back into the model.
editorial.whats_new: RSI now has a second science benchmark and its first robotics loop: RecurSciBench (Nov 24) tests whether agents' self-improvement transfers to new tasks, and RoboEvo² (Nov 25) has a coding agent and a VLA policy improve each other.
editorial.why_it_matters: Self-improving loops now edit harnesses, weights, and robot policies, so the harness and every self-edit become versioned artifacts that need held-out evals, transfer checks, and rollback.
editorial.take_for_builders: If your agent edits its own prompts, tools, memory, or weights, version every self-edit and gate it on a held-out eval of unseen tasks, with a rollback path, before it reaches production.

storylines.label: Inference GPU
storylines.latest_title: The model inside the server: Network design for inference on a few GPU nodes

editorial.tldr: This is a loose topic cluster about running inference on GPUs, not one event. Its main thread is AWS adding managed ways to share one GPU: NVIDIA MIG partitions for SageMaker endpoints on Nov 6, then Lambda GPU functions with up to 48 concurrent invocations per model on Nov 22.
editorial.whats_new: An APNIC design guide for self-hosted inference on a few GPU nodes, built on a 4-server, 8-GPU vLLM setup running Llama 3.3 70B, argues that request handling and session count matter more than GPU-to-GPU bandwidth.
editorial.why_it_matters: Whether you rent shared GPUs from AWS or run a few nodes yourself, utilization now depends on how requests are batched and routed more than on raw interconnect speed.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before buying faster interconnect for a small self-hosted cluster, load-test request concurrency and session counts on vLLM; for bursty small models, benchmark SageMaker MIG and Lambda GPU first.
